Note: The user running the code needs to update file paths. The data that is retrieved comes in the form of a text file and is saved into the “inputs” folder. Subsequent code writes the data to csv files into the “outputs2” folder.

# Initialize variables for API request
dsource = 'zbp'
ecols = 'ESTAB,EMP,EMPSZES,GEO_ID,ZIPCODE,PAYQTR1,PAYANN'
api_key = 'da5ca696289b328bc3575a3405c6196767cb452c'
naics = '445310' # Note: You can update the NAICS code to import other industry data


# Updated to change census year depending on calendar year of data

# Define the path to the "input" folder relative to the user's home directory. 
# This is where the data retrieved from the API request will be stored.
user_home = os.path.expanduser("~")
input_folder = os.path.join(user_home, 'OneDrive - Colostate', 'Teaching', 'Courses', 'CSU', 'AREC570', 'api_docs', 'zbp_data', 'input')
print(input_folder)

# Define the mapping of years to nyear
year_to_nyear = {
    2000: 1997,
    2001: 1997,
    2002: 2002,
    2003: 2002,
    2004: 2002,
    2005: 2002,
    2006: 2002,
    2007: 2007,
    2008: 2007,
    2009: 2007,
    2010: 2007,
    2011: 2007,
    2012: 2012,
    2013: 2012,
    2014: 2012,
    2015: 2012,
    2016: 2012,
    2017: 2017,
    2018: 2017
}

# Loop through years and set nyear accordingly
for year in range(2000, 2019):
    nyear = year_to_nyear[year]
    base_url = f'https://api.census.gov/data/{year}/{dsource}'
    edata_url = f'{base_url}?get={ecols}&NAICS{nyear}={naics}&for=zipcode:*&key={api_key}'
    
    # Use edata_url for the desired API request or further processing
    print(f'For year {year}, nyear is {nyear}, and edata_url is: {edata_url}')
    
    # Make an API request, retrieve data, and save to a file
    a = requests.get(edata_url)
    quote = a.text
    outpath = os.path.join(input_folder, f'Out{year}_NAICS{naics}.txt')
    with open(outpath, 'w', encoding='utf-8') as f:
        f.write(quote)
        
    print(outpath)


# Specify the input folder and output folder
user_home = os.path.expanduser("~")
output_folder = os.path.join(user_home, 'OneDrive - Colostate', 'Teaching', 'Courses', 'CSU', 'AREC570', 'api_docs', 'zbp_data', 'output')
print(output_folder)

# Function to remove brackets from a list
def remove_brackets(lst):
    return [item.strip('[]"') for item in lst]

# Loop through the text files in the input folder
for filename in os.listdir(input_folder):
    if filename.endswith(".txt"):
        # Construct the full file paths
        input_file = os.path.join(input_folder, filename)
        output_file = os.path.join(output_folder, os.path.splitext(filename)[0] + ".csv")

        # Open the input text file for reading
        with open(input_file, 'r', newline='', encoding='utf-8') as txt_file:
            # Read the data from the text file and remove brackets
            data = [remove_brackets(row) for row in csv.reader(txt_file)]
            
            # Print the top 5 rows
            print(f'Top 5 rows of {filename}:')
            for row in data[:5]:
                print(row)

            # Open the corresponding output CSV file for writing
            with open(output_file, 'w', newline='', encoding='utf-8') as csv_file:
                # Write the data to the CSV file
                csv.writer(csv_file).writerows(data)

        print(f'Converted {filename} to {os.path.basename(output_file)}')

print("Conversion complete.")

title: Lecture 7.1: Reviewing Research
text:
The reviewer’s job
Help the editor assess the paper and help the author understand its strengths and weaknesses.

Identify the contribution.
Assess the evidence and reasoning.
Distinguish essential revisions from optional improvements.
Explain the recommendation.

title: Lecture 7.1: Reviewing Research
text:
Where the report fits
A typical sequence:

Submission and editorial screening.
Invitation to reviewers.
Reports and editorial decision.
Revision, rejection, or acceptance.

Procedures vary by journal. Follow the instructions for the specific review.

title: Lecture 7.1: Reviewing Research
section: Evaluate the paper in front of you
text:
Evaluate the paper in front of you

Engage with its question and intended contribution.
Do not require the author to write your preferred different paper.
Explain problems rather than merely declaring them.
Be direct and constructive.

Source: Berk et al. (2015).

title: Lecture 7.1: Reviewing Research
text:
AJAE: several dimensions of merit
The assigned criteria address:

Contribution and originality.
Scholarship and analysis.
Appeal to the readership.
Appropriate illustrations and length.

A report should explain how the paper meets or falls short of relevant criteria.
Source: Agricultural and Applied Economics Association (2013).

title: Lecture 7.1: Reviewing Research
text:
Ethridge: follow the argument

Is the objective clear?
Does the sequence of ideas lead toward it?
Does the organization help the reader?
Are important terms precise and consistent?
Which general problem matters more than sentence-level edits?

Source: Ethridge (2004).

title: Lecture 7.1: Reviewing Research
text:
Discussion: identify the binding weakness
A paper has a clear question, polished prose, and precise estimates, but its comparison group is exposed to the treatment.

Which review criterion is affected?
Why does the concern matter?
What evidence or revision could address it?
When would this be fatal to the paper’s main claim?

Hypothetical review exercise.

title: Lecture 7.1: Reviewing Research
text:
Structure a referee report

Brief summary of question, method, and main contribution.
Overall assessment.
Major comments, ordered by importance.
Specific comments with locations.
Recommendation communicated as the journal requests.

A summary demonstrates understanding; it should not dominate the report.

title: Lecture 7.1: Reviewing Research
text:
Make a major comment actionable

Which standards overlap?
Which apply mainly to work not yet completed?
How should uncertainty about feasibility affect a proposal review?
How would you revise your proposal after this comparison?

A reasoned overall assessment.

title: Lecture 6.4: Experiments, Qualitative and Mixed Methods
text:
Falk and Heckman: controlled variation
Laboratory experiments let researchers vary features of a decision environment.
They can separate mechanisms that move together in observational settings.
A simplified setting can be informative when it isolates a relevant mechanism.
Source: Falk and Heckman (2009).

title: Lecture 6.4: Experiments, Qualitative and Mixed Methods
text:

What does the reading mean by controlled variation?
Is visual resemblance to everyday life the same as external validity?
What can the gift-exchange example reveal?
Which features would you vary to examine whether a result travels?

title: Lecture 6.4: Experiments, Qualitative and Mixed Methods
section: Qualitative does not simply mean words
text:
Qualitative does not simply mean words
Starr emphasizes an open-ended approach to gathering information.
Rather than fixing every relevant dimension in advance, researchers allow new themes and explanations to emerge.
Clear questions and systematic procedures still matter.
Source: Starr (2014).

title: Lecture 6.4: Experiments, Qualitative and Mixed Methods
text:
Methods and their uses



Method
What it can reveal




In-depth interview
Reasoning and experience


Focus group
Shared and contested interpretations


Case study or site visit

Fieldwork

Life history

title: Lecture 6.4: Experiments, Qualitative and Mixed Methods
section: Ask a different kind of question
text:
Ask a different kind of question
Closed question:

Which listed factor mattered most in buying your home?

Open question:

Tell me how you came to buy this home.

What could the second reveal that the first excludes? What makes the answers harder to analyze?

title: Lecture 6.4: Experiments, Qualitative and Mixed Methods
section: Why ask people about their decisions?
text:
Why ask people about their decisions?
The source slides discuss interviews about wage and price rigidity.
Interviews can help distinguish mechanisms that aggregate data leave unresolved.
But respondents may not know, remember, or fully explain their motivations.

Preserves the source discussion of Bewley and Blinder. The source speaker notes use Friedman’s billiard-player analogy: competent action does not require the ability to articulate a formal model.

title: Lecture 6.4: Experiments, Qualitative and Mixed Methods
text:
Credibility in qualitative work

Document recruitment and protocols.
Explain coding and interpretation.
Reflect on the researcher’s role.
Seek evidence that challenges emerging explanations.
Cross-check accounts against other sources.

Source: Starr (2014).

title: Lecture 6.4: Experiments, Qualitative and Mixed Methods
text:
Self-reports require interpretation
Potential concerns include recall, incentives, social desirability, and limited self-knowledge.
Responses can still be informative.
Ask which claim a response supports and what additional evidence would strengthen it.

title: Lecture 6.4: Experiments, Qualitative and Mixed Methods
text:
Three mixed-methods sequences

Qualitative first: discover concepts and design a structured instrument.
Quantitative first: follow up to understand patterns or unexpected results.
Concurrent: compare and integrate evidence collected in parallel.

Explain how the components inform one another.

title: Lecture 6.2: Causality and Policy Evaluation
section: Separate the target from the tool
text:
Separate the target from the tool

Estimand: the quantity we want to learn.
Estimator: the rule used to estimate it from data.
Estimate: the numerical result in our sample.

Example: an average treatment effect, a difference-in-means estimator, and its estimated value.

title: Lecture 6.2: Causality and Policy Evaluation
text:
What creates a credible comparison?
For every design, ask:

Who is compared with whom?
What creates the difference in treatment?
What must be true of the untreated counterfactual?
To which population does the result apply?

Source: Athey and Imbens (2017).

title: Lecture 6.2: Causality and Policy Evaluation
text:
Regression discontinuity
Treatment changes at a threshold in a running variable.

Compare observations close to the cutoff.
Ask whether other determinants of the outcome change smoothly.
Check for manipulation and other policies at the same threshold.
Interpret the effect locally.

title: Lecture 6.2: Causality and Policy Evaluation
text:
Sharp and fuzzy designs

Sharp RD: treatment status changes deterministically at the threshold.
Fuzzy RD: the probability of treatment changes.

In a fuzzy design, divide the outcome discontinuity by the treatment discontinuity, with additional assumptions for a local causal interpretation.
A weak treatment discontinuity makes inference difficult.

title: Lecture 6.2: Causality and Policy Evaluation
text:
Discussion: summer school
The source example assigns summer school using a test-score threshold.

Identify the running variable, cutoff, treatment, and outcome.
Why compare students close to the cutoff?
Could students or schools influence their position?
What would limit generalization to all students?

title: Lecture 6.2: Causality and Policy Evaluation
text:
Difference-in-differences
τ̂=(Y‾T,post−Y‾T,pre)−(Y‾C,post−Y‾C,pre)
\hat\tau =
(\bar Y_{T,\mathrm{post}}-\bar Y_{T,\mathrm{pre}})
-
(\bar Y_{C,\mathrm{post}}-\bar Y_{C,\mathrm{pre}})

The comparison group supplies a counterfactual change.
The key assumption concerns parallel untreated trends, not identical outcome levels.

title: Lecture 6.2: Causality and Policy Evaluation
text:
Assess the DiD argument

Why should untreated trends be comparable?
Are there anticipatory responses?
Did another policy change at the same time?
Did group composition change?
Could treatment spill over to the comparison group?

Similar pre-trends are useful evidence, not proof of the identifying assumption.

title: Lecture 6.2: Causality and Policy Evaluation
text:
Synthetic control
Construct a weighted comparison from untreated units.

Choose weights using pre-intervention information.
Assess pre-intervention fit.
Examine the post-intervention gap.
Investigate donor contamination and sensitivity.

A close pre-treatment fit does not by itself establish causality.

title: Lecture 6.2: Causality and Policy Evaluation
text:
Discussion: choose a design
A policy begins in one region, with several years of data before and after.

What would support DiD?
What would make synthetic control attractive?
Would a threshold design be available?
Which additional institutional information do you need?

Do not select a method only because software can estimate it.

title: Lecture 6.2: Causality and Policy Evaluation
text:
Placebos probe specific threats
A placebo asks whether the design finds an effect where the proposed mechanism predicts none.
Examples:

A false treatment date before the intervention.
An outcome that should not respond.
Predetermined characteristics at an RD cutoff.

Explain why each placebo is informative.

Preserves the lottery example from source slide 38: compare large and small prize winners, then ask whether future winnings predict pre-treatment earnings. For RD, examine discontinuities in predetermined covariates rather than requiring unconditional independence from treatment.

title: Lecture 6.2: Causality and Policy Evaluation
text:
Robustness and sensitivity
Change a justified modeling or design choice and explain what that change tests.

Alternative bandwidth.
Alternative comparison group.
Alternative measurement.
Alternative functional form.

Report informative disagreements. Avoid searching for a specification that preserves a preferred result.

title: Lecture 6.2: Causality and Policy Evaluation
text:

Choose one recommendation from Athey and Imbens.

Which identifying assumption does it probe?
What result would reduce your confidence?
What can the check not establish?
How would you report a failure?

title: Lecture 6.2: Causality and Policy Evaluation
text:
Workshop: a credibility checklist
For your design, propose:

One placebo.
One sensitivity analysis.
One external-validity limitation.

State the threat each item addresses.

title: Lecture 6.2: Causality and Policy Evaluation
text:

Provider and dataset.
Collection purpose and method.
Release or retrieval date.
Geographic and time coverage.
Access conditions relevant to replication.

Define the unit of observation
“County data” is not enough.
Is one row a county, county-year, county-industry-year, or county-month?

Units and reference period.
Transformation.
Interpretation.

Which identifiers were used?
What matching relationship was expected?
How many records failed to match?
Did merging duplicate observations?
How were finer observations aggregated?

What does the sample look like?
How much relevant variation is present?
Are extreme values plausible?
Do treatment and comparison groups differ?

How would a collaborator discover the edit?
What happens when new data arrive?
Could you explain the change six months later?
Which parts of your workflow rely on memory?

title: Lecture 5.3: Managing Data for Reproducibility: Git I
text:
Automate the sequence
A main script expresses the order of operations.
# Run from the project root.
source("code/01_clean.R")
source("code/02_analyze.R")
source("code/03_tables.R")
Each step reads documented inputs and writes predictable outputs.

title: Lecture 5.3: Managing Data for Reproducibility: Git I
text:
Separate files by function
project/
  README.md
  run.R
  code/
  data/
    raw/
    derived/
  output/
    tables/
    figures/
Keep raw inputs unchanged. Regenerate derived files through code.

title: Lecture 5.3: Managing Data for Reproducibility: Git I
section: Paths should travel with the project
text:
Paths should travel with the project
Prefer paths relative to the project root:
read.csv("data/raw/survey.csv")
A path containing your user directory will usually fail on another computer.
State where the main script should be run.

title: Lecture 5.3: Managing Data for Reproducibility: Git I
text:
What Git records
Git records selected snapshots and the history connecting them.

Working directory: files you are editing.
Staging area: changes selected for the next snapshot.
Commit: recorded snapshot and message.

GitHub hosts repositories and supports collaboration. Git also works locally.

title: Lecture 5.3: Managing Data for Reproducibility: Git I
section: First commit in a practice folder
text:
First commit in a practice folder
git init
git status
git add README.md run.R code/
git diff --staged
git commit -m "Add reproducible analysis workflow"
Inspect staged changes before committing.

New exercise. Use a separate practice folder containing these files. Git may request author name and email on first use.

title: Lecture 5.3: Managing Data for Reproducibility: Git I
text:
The everyday loop

Make one coherent change.
Inspect it with git diff.
Stage the relevant files.
Inspect with git diff --staged.
Commit with a meaningful message.

git status
git log --oneline

title: Lecture 5.3: Managing Data for Reproducibility: Git I
text:
Write a useful commit message
Weak: “updates”
Better: “Distinguish refused responses from zeros”
Explain why a change affects the sample or interpretation when that is not obvious.
A commit should make sense to someone who was not watching you work.

title: Lecture 5.3: Managing Data for Reproducibility: Git I
text:
What belongs outside the repository?
Common exclusions:

Credentials and local configuration.
Confidential or restricted data.
Large raw-data files.
Reproducible temporary outputs.

A .gitignore file prevents matching untracked files from being added by default. It does not remove already tracked files.

title: Lecture 5.1: Data Collection: Surveys

Primary and secondary data







Primary
Secondary




Collected for your research purpose
Collected for another purpose


More control over instrument and sampling
Often lower acquisition cost


Responsibility for collection quality
Responsibility for understanding provenance and limitations



Neither category guarantees valid measurement.

title: Lecture 5.1: Data Collection: Surveys

Who collected the data, and for what purpose?
What incentives did respondents and collectors face?
What checks were performed?
What documentation would allow you to assess quality?

An unfamiliar value can be an error, a coding convention, or an important observation.

title: Lecture 5.1: Data Collection: Surveys

Define the population and frame

Target population: the group about which you want to make claims.
Sampling frame: the list or mechanism used to reach that group.
Sample: selected units.
Respondents: selected units from whom data are obtained.

Example: a homeowner list will not cover all residents if renters matter.

section: Nonresponse is more than a small sample
text:
Nonresponse is more than a small sample

A low response rate reduces the amount of information.
Bias depends on how response relates to the outcome.
Compare available respondent characteristics with the frame.
Such comparisons cannot rule out differences on unobserved characteristics.

Who might be missing from a survey of recreational users?

title: Lecture 5.1: Data Collection: Surveys
text:
Weights and uncertainty

Unequal selection probabilities may require weights.
Nonresponse adjustments depend on assumptions.
Standard errors should account for the survey design where relevant.
A large sample does not repair an incorrect sampling frame.

title: Lecture 5.1: Data Collection: Surveys
text:
Write questions people can answer

Ask about one concept at a time.
Specify the reference period.
Use clear, consistent response options.
Avoid leading wording.
Pretest how respondents interpret the question.

Source: Champ (2017).

How many concepts are combined?

Mode and administration

Interviewers can clarify questions but may influence responses.
Self-administered surveys provide privacy but less clarification.
Online recruitment changes who is reached and who participates.
Plan consent, confidentiality, and institutional review before collection.

Adapted from Unit 4, slides 3–6. Ask students to describe their mechanism before naming an estimator.

title: Lecture 4.1: Conceptual Framework and Theory
section: A model is a deliberate simplification
text:
A model is a deliberate simplification
A useful model leaves things out. The question is whether it leaves out something essential to the argument.

Which details are necessary for the mechanism?
Which assumptions make the analysis manageable?
Which conclusions would change if an assumption failed?

A regression coefficient alone does not explain a causal mechanism.

title: Lecture 4.1: Conceptual Framework and Theory
section: From a problem to a model
text:
From a problem to a model
Following Ethridge:

Locate the problem in the literature.
Strip it down to the relevant choices and constraints.
Start with a simple theoretical structure.
Add the features needed for this question.
Derive hypotheses and identify the evidence needed to assess them.

Source: Ethridge (2004).

title: Lecture 4.1: Conceptual Framework and Theory
text:
Ask Varian’s questions

Who makes the choices?
What do these agents want?
How do they interact?
What constraints do they face?
What adjusts when their choices are inconsistent?

Discussion: Which answer is least clear in your proposed project?
Source: Varian (1997), assigned pp. 4–6.

title: Lecture 4.1: Conceptual Framework and Theory
section: Example: irrigation under a water price
text:
Example: irrigation under a water price
Illustrative classroom model: A farmer chooses water use ww.
maxw≥0pf(w)−cw
\max_{w\geq 0}\; p f(w)-cw


p>0p>0: output price.
c>0c>0: price per unit of water.
f(w)f(w): production, with f′(w)>0f'(w)>0 and f″(w)<0f''(w)<0.

For an interior optimum, pf′(w*)=cpf'(w^*)=c.

text:
Derive the prediction
Differentiating the first-order condition gives
pf″(w*)dw*dc=1⇒dw*dc=1pf″(w*)<0.
p f''(w^*)\frac{dw^*}{dc}=1
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\frac{dw^*}{dc}=\frac{1}{p f''(w^*)}<0.

Conditional prediction: Higher water prices reduce optimal water use.
Which assumptions make the sign follow? What changes if water use is fixed by a binding quota?

New classroom example. Hold output price, technology, and other inputs fixed. The derivative assumes a differentiable, strictly concave production function and an interior solution.

title: Lecture 4.1: Conceptual Framework and Theory
text:
Discussion: Ethridge and Varian

How does simplifying a problem help us understand it?
At what point does simplification remove the mechanism we care about?
Would the irrigation model answer a question about farm income, water use, or both?
What additional structure would an income question require?

Bring one assumption from your own project into the discussion.

title: Lecture 4.1: Conceptual Framework and Theory
text:
Cheng: discovery and exposition
Finding an argument and presenting it are different tasks.
A readable proof states:

Definitions and assumptions.
A sequence of justified steps.
The conclusion that those steps establish.

Source: Cheng (2004).

title: Lecture 4.1: Conceptual Framework and Theory
text:
Discussion: find the missing step
A student writes:

Water becomes more expensive, so farmers adopt efficient irrigation, and total water use falls.


Which part describes a choice? Which part is a prediction?
Could adoption change irrigated acreage or crop choice?
What assumptions are needed to conclude that total water use falls?
Rewrite the argument so each conclusion follows from a stated premise.


New exercise applying Cheng’s guidance. This is a hypothetical claim to diagnose, not a claim about observed irrigation outcomes.

title: Lecture 4.1: Conceptual Framework and Theory
text:
What Romer calls mathiness
Romer challenges arguments in which the connection between formal symbols, verbal claims, and economic meaning becomes unclear.

Do the terms mean the same thing throughout the argument?
Does the mathematical result support the verbal conclusion?
Can the assumptions and derivation be checked?

Source: Romer (2015).

title: Lecture 4.1: Conceptual Framework and Theory
text:
Discussion: evaluate Romer’s argument

What specific example does Romer use to support his criticism?
How does he distinguish mathematical theory from mathiness?
Which claims concern the models, and which concern incentives in the profession?
What evidence would make you revise your assessment of his argument?

Support your answer with a passage from the reading.

The source deck frames several contested interpretations as conclusions. This discussion asks students to assess those interpretations against the paper.

title: Lecture 4.1: Conceptual Framework and Theory
section: A check against our own biases
text:
A check against our own biases

Am I choosing assumptions because they clarify the problem or deliver a preferred result?
Have I separated a model implication from an empirical claim?
Would I accept the same argument if its conclusion were inconvenient?
What criticism would improve the framework?

title: Lecture 4.1: Conceptual Framework and Theory
text:
Listen for the implicit model
At a seminar, identify:

The agents and their incentives.
The mechanism linking the explanatory variable to the outcome.
The assumptions connecting the evidence to that mechanism.

Then ask a question about a specific missing link.

Research question.
Agents, choices, and constraints.
Mechanism.
Testable prediction.
One assumption that could fail.

Exchange with a partner. Mark the step that needs the most explanation.

“My model predicts ___ because ___.”
“That prediction depends on ___.”

section: Theory in theoretical and empirical papers
text:
Theory in theoretical and empirical papers







Theoretical contribution
Empirical contribution




Develop or modify a model
Explain the mechanism behind the empirical question


Establish analytical results
Derive the hypotheses to be evaluated


Show what changes relative to existing theory
Connect theoretical concepts to measured variables



Both require explicit assumptions and a coherent argument.
Source: Chouinard (2015).

title: Lecture 4.2: Reporting the Conceptual Framework
text:
Build the argument in order

Explain the relationship to existing theory.
Define agents, choices, and the feasible set.
State assumptions.
Present the objective or relevant relationships.
Explain the derivation.
Interpret the result and connect it to the question.

Avoid making readers infer a missing step.

title: Lecture 4.2: Reporting the Conceptual Framework
text:
Definitions, assumptions, and results

A definition tells readers what a term means.
An assumption specifies what the argument takes as given.
A proposition states a result established from those premises.
A corollary follows from an established result.

Labeling a claim “Proposition” does not establish it.
Source: Chouinard (2015).

title: Lecture 4.2: Reporting the Conceptual Framework
text:
Make equations readable

Introduce each symbol.
State the domain and units when relevant.
Explain what changes and what stays fixed.
Follow a mathematical result with its economic interpretation.
Put lengthy derivations in an appendix when they interrupt the argument.

title: Lecture 4.2: Reporting the Conceptual Framework
text:
Discussion: Chouinard’s advice

Which guidance applies equally to theoretical and empirical papers?
When should a familiar model be summarized rather than derived?
What does a reader need before seeing the first equation?
Choose one recommendation and explain how it would improve your draft.

title: Lecture 4.2: Reporting the Conceptual Framework
section: From a prediction to a measurement
text:
From a prediction to a measurement
Return to the irrigation example.








Model concept
Possible empirical measure
Question to resolve




Water price
Marginal charge per unit
Is there a fixed fee or tiered rate?


Water use
Metered withdrawals
Do withdrawals equal crop consumption?


Technology
Irrigation system
Can adoption change with the price?



A theoretical variable and its proxy are rarely interchangeable without explanation.

title: Lecture 4.2: Reporting the Conceptual Framework
text:
Identification asks a different question
The framework explains why a relationship might exist.
Identification asks what evidence distinguishes that relationship from competing explanations.
For water prices and use:

Do more water-scarce places set higher prices?
Do weather and prices move together?
Do farmers select into different pricing arrangements?

title: Lecture 4.2: Reporting the Conceptual Framework
text:
Common threats

Omitted variables: another factor affects both the explanatory variable and outcome.
Reverse causality: the outcome helps determine the explanatory variable.
Selection: compared groups differ for reasons related to the outcome.

Naming a regression method does not resolve these threats.

title: Lecture 4.2: Reporting the Conceptual Framework

The slides discuss airport pollution and health:

Nearby exposure varies with location, wind, and airport activity.
Local weather may affect both pollution and health.
Congestion elsewhere in the airport network is proposed as another source of variation.

Discussion: What would have to be true for distant congestion to be useful for identification?

“The model predicts …”

Suggest one revision that makes the logic easier to follow.

text:
What is an API?
An application programming interface provides a defined way for one program to request information from another.
A data request typically specifies:

Dataset and period.
Variables.
Geography or other filters.
Authentication, when required.

The response must still be interpreted and validated.

title: Lecture 5.2: Data Collection via API

A reproducible retrieval workflow

Read the dataset documentation.
Specify a small request.
Save the raw response.
Check the schema, units, and codes.
Transform into an analysis-ready table.
Record the request and retrieval date.

section: A successful request is not a valid dataset
text:
A successful request is not a valid dataset

Does each row describe a business, ZIP code, or ZIP-by-industry cell?
Are quantities counts, rates, or monetary values?
Are zeros distinguishable from suppressed or missing observations?
Are industry definitions comparable across years?
Are identifiers preserved as text where leading zeros matter?

[

Record the retrieval

Dataset name and version, if provided.
Query parameters and variable definitions.
Retrieval date.
Geography and classification vintage.
Raw file location.
Transformations and validation checks.

Store credentials separately from shared code.

When bulk downloads are better
A bulk file may be preferable when:

You need most of a dataset.
Repeated requests are slow or restricted.
A fixed release is easier to archive and reproduce.

Choose an access method that gives a reliable, documented snapshot.

Dominitz and Manski: the decision problem
With a fixed budget, compare collection methods that differ in cost and information quality.
The paper studies less expensive methods with:

Nonresponse, or
Coarser interval measurements.

More observations do not automatically remove incomplete information.

  1000 * events / population

When is a function clearer than repeated code?
When does a general solution become harder to understand?
What would make a function easier to check?
Which repeated step in your project is worth simplifying?

Source: Gentzkow and Shapiro (2014), Section 6.

title: Lecture 5.4: Managing Data for Reproducibility: Git II

Documentation explains decisions
Use names and structure to show what code does.
Use comments for:

Why a choice was made.
A source or definition.
An unexpected but intentional rule.
A limitation a future user might miss.

A codebook should define units and missing-value conventions.

title: Lecture 5.4: Managing Data for Reproducibility: Git II
text:
A task needs an owner
A useful task record contains:

A concrete deliverable.
One responsible person.
Inputs and dependencies.
A definition of completion.
A place to record decisions.

What goes wrong in the reading’s email exchange about robustness checks?
Source: Gentzkow and Shapiro (2014), Section 8.

A branch for a focused change
In the practice repository:

Use the actual default branch name if it is not main.

A conflict requires a decision

Read both versions and understand their intentions.
Edit the file to the agreed result.
Remove conflict markers.
Check the result, stage it, and complete the merge.

Do not choose a version solely because it is newer.

title: Lecture 5.4: Managing Data for Reproducibility: Git II

Code style supports review

Use meaningful names.
Keep indentation consistent.
Separate distinct operations.
Prefer readable expressions.
Avoid repeated unexplained numbers.

Which style rule prevents a plausible research error?

title: Lecture 6.1: Econometric Models and Identification
text:
Start with four questions

What relationship are you trying to learn about?
What would the ideal experiment look like?
What identification strategy is feasible?
How will you quantify uncertainty?

Source: Angrist and Pischke (2009).

title: Lecture 6.1: Econometric Models and Identification
text:
Structural and reduced-form approaches







Structural
Reduced-form / design-based




Specifies behavioral relationships
Focuses on variation identifying an effect


Recovers parameters within a model
Often targets a treatment or policy effect


Can support model-based counterfactuals
Often speaks most directly to the studied setting



Both require assumptions. Their usefulness depends on the question.
Source: Timmins and Schlenker (2009).

title: Lecture 6.1: Econometric Models and Identification
text:
What a structural model adds

Agents, objectives, constraints, and interactions.
Parameters with a behavioral interpretation.
A way to trace feedback and equilibrium responses.
A framework for welfare or unobserved policy counterfactuals.

Identification still requires informative data and defensible restrictions.

title: Lecture 6.1: Econometric Models and Identification
text:
Example: vehicle policy
The source slides use fuel-economy regulation versus fuel taxation.
A model may need:

Firms’ new-vehicle decisions.
Household vehicle choice and driving.
Used-vehicle markets and scrappage.
Interactions across these decisions.

Which effects would a simple comparison of new-car fuel economy miss?

Adapted from Unit 6, slides 6–8 and the discussion of Jacobsen in Timmins and Schlenker. Focus on the mechanism rather than presenting uncited numerical results.

title: Lecture 6.1: Econometric Models and Identification
text:
Structural tradeoffs
Potential gains: explicit mechanisms, feedbacks, welfare analysis, counterfactual simulation.
Challenges: specification, computational demands, identification, and sensitivity to behavioral assumptions.
A counterfactual prediction is conditional on the model remaining appropriate.

title: Lecture 6.1: Econometric Models and Identification
text:
What reduced-form designs emphasize

A clearly defined outcome and treatment.
A credible comparison.
Institutional knowledge about assignment.
Variation that isolates the relationship of interest.

Fixed effects, thresholds, instruments, and random assignment are possible tools, not automatic guarantees.

title: Lecture 6.1: Econometric Models and Identification
text:
Discussion: Timmins and Schlenker
For your proposed question:

Is the goal an effect in an observed setting or a new policy counterfactual?
Which behavioral responses must be represented?
Which assumptions would each approach require?
Could the approaches provide complementary evidence?

title: Lecture 6.1: Econometric Models and Identification
text:
Outcomes we cannot observe together
Let Yi(1)Y_i(1) be an individual’s outcome under treatment and Yi(0)Y_i(0) under no treatment.
Yi=DiYi(1)+(1−Di)Yi(0)
Y_i=D_iY_i(1)+(1-D_i)Y_i(0)

We observe only one potential outcome for each individual.
The missing counterfactual is the central problem.

title: Lecture 6.1: Econometric Models and Identification
text:
Selection contaminates a raw comparison
E[Y∣D=1]−E[Y∣D=0]=E[Y(1)−Y(0)∣D=1]+E[Y(0)∣D=1]−E[Y(0)∣D=0].
\begin{aligned}
E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]
&=E[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid D=1]\\
&\quad+E[Y(0)\mid D=1]-E[Y(0)\mid D=0].
\end{aligned}

The first term is the average treatment effect on the treated. The remaining difference is selection bias.

title: Lecture 6.1: Econometric Models and Identification
text:
Example: hospitals and health
People who visit hospitals may have worse health than those who do not.

Does that establish that hospitals worsen health?
What would their health have been without treatment?
Which selection process makes the raw comparison misleading?

Source: Angrist and Pischke (2009).

title: Lecture 6.1: Econometric Models and Identification
text:
What random assignment gives us
Under random assignment:
D⟂(Y(0),Y(1)).
D\;\perp\;(Y(0),Y(1)).

With consistency and no interference, the population difference in means identifies the average treatment effect.
Randomization makes groups comparable in expectation; a realized sample can still be imbalanced.

Corrects Unit 6, slide 24: assignment is independent of potential outcomes, not necessarily of the observed outcome. Imperfect compliance and attrition require additional analysis.

title: Lecture 6.1: Econometric Models and Identification
section: Regression does not remove selection by itself
text:
Regression does not remove selection by itself
In a model such as
Yi=α+τDi+Xi′β+εi,Y_i=\alpha+\tau D_i+X_i'\beta+\varepsilon_i,
a causal interpretation of τ\tau needs assumptions about treatment assignment and the error term.
Controls can help with comparability or precision. They can also introduce problems if chosen without a causal argument.

title: Lecture 6.1: Econometric Models and Identification
text:
Read the experimental table



Table from Mostly Harmless Econometrics comparing estimated small-class effects across specifications with additional controls.


Source: Angrist and Pischke; retained from Unit 6, slide 26.

title: Lecture 6.1: Econometric Models and Identification
text:
Discussion: what changes across columns?

Which coefficients are stable?
What happens to standard errors?
How can controls improve precision in an experiment?
What would a large change in the treatment coefficient prompt you to investigate?

Start with the table’s sample, units, and assignment process.

title: Lecture 6.1: Econometric Models and Identification
text:
Omitted-variable bias
Suppose the population model is
Y=α+βX+γZ+u,Y=\alpha+\beta X+\gamma Z+u,
but we omit ZZ. Under the usual exogeneity conditions,
plim⁡β̂short=β+γCov⁡(X,Z)Var⁡(X).
\operatorname{plim}\hat\beta_{\text{short}}
=\beta+\gamma\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Z)}{\operatorname{Var}(X)}.

Both the outcome relevance of ZZ and its association with XX matter.

title: Lecture 6.1: Econometric Models and Identification
text:
Discussion: Jurajda

Where does the relevant variation come from?
Why is a simple group comparison insufficient?
What institutional detail supports the design?

title: Lecture 6.1: Econometric Models and Identification
section: Can you describe the ideal experiment?
text:
Can you describe the ideal experiment?
Specify treatment, population, assignment, outcome, and follow-up period.
If the treatment itself is ambiguous, refine the question first.

Preserves the source speaker-note example: changing school-start age may also change schooling duration or age at testing. Ask students which effect their hypothetical experiment would isolate.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
text:
Begin with the task
Are we trying to:

Predict an outcome?
Describe patterns?
Estimate a causal effect?
Learn how effects vary?

The task determines how success should be evaluated.
Source: Athey and Imbens (2019).

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
text:
Prediction and causality
A model can predict outcomes well using variables that do not cause them.
A causal question asks how outcomes change under an intervention.
Predictive accuracy alone does not justify changing a policy variable.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
text:
Supervised and unsupervised learning

Supervised: learn a relationship between inputs and observed outcomes.
Unsupervised: find structure without an outcome label.

Examples: predicting demand versus grouping similar observations.
Both can contribute to economic research when the role is explicit.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
text:
Overfitting
A flexible model can fit noise in its training sample.

Evaluate performance on observations not used to fit the model.
Keep the final test set separate from model selection.
Respect the dependence structure when splitting data.

For forecasting, information from the future should not enter training.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
text:
Bias and variance
Greater flexibility may reduce approximation bias while increasing variability.
Regularization constrains the fit to improve performance outside the training sample.
The best training fit is not necessarily the best predictive model.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
text:
LASSO
A common form minimizes
1n∑i=1n(Yi−α−Xi′β)2+λ∑j=1p|βj|.
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(Y_i-\alpha-X_i'\beta)^2
+\lambda\sum_{j=1}^{p}|\beta_j|.


The penalty shrinks coefficients and may set some to zero.
The tuning parameter controls the penalty.
Cross-validation can guide predictive tuning.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
text:
Trees and forests
A regression tree splits observations into groups with different predicted outcomes.
A random forest averages predictions across many randomized trees.



Illustrative regression tree with splitting rules and terminal-node predictions, retained from the source deck.


Source: Unit 6, slide 43.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
text:
Exercise: identify leakage
A model predicts whether a household will miss a payment.
One input is “number of collection calls made during the following month.”

Why might this variable predict well?
Could it be known at prediction time?
How would you redesign the evaluation?

This is a hypothetical example.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
text:
Model selection and confounding
Selecting variables only for predicting the outcome can omit variables important for treatment assignment.
The reading discusses selecting predictors of both outcome and treatment, then using their union in an appropriate estimation procedure.
This still depends on the underlying identification assumptions.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: Machine learning within a causal design
text:
Machine learning within a causal design
Flexible methods may estimate nuisance relationships such as:

Expected outcomes conditional on covariates.
Treatment probabilities.

Sample splitting and specialized inference can help manage overfitting.
Machine learning does not supply exogenous variation by itself.

title: Lecture 6.5: Evaluating Empirical Evidence
text:
Credibility involves more than identification
A strong design can still estimate a quantity different from the one the researcher intends.
Check:

Research question.
Estimand.
Measurement.
Population.
Interpretation.

Source: Gibson (2019).

title: Lecture 6.5: Evaluating Empirical Evidence
section: Does the measure match the concept?
text:
Does the measure match the concept?

Does a registry describe residents or registered persons?
Does expenditure reflect quantity, quality, or both?
Does infrequent recall obscure variation within a period?
Does aggregation hide the response of interest?

Institutional knowledge of the data matters.

title: Lecture 6.5: Evaluating Empirical Evidence
text:
Avoid discarding information unnecessarily
A continuous measure can be converted into an indicator, but that discards information.
Example: income versus an indicator for income below a poverty threshold.
Explain why the indicator matches the question. Consider how measurement error near the cutoff changes classification.

title: Lecture 6.5: Evaluating Empirical Evidence
text:
Spatial processes cross boundaries
A policy in one area may affect neighbors.

Does the outcome depend on nearby exposure?
Could the comparison group be affected?
Does the estimated effect include spillovers?
Does aggregation hide them?

Match the model and interpretation to the spatial process.

title: Lecture 6.5: Evaluating Empirical Evidence
text:
Discussion: Gibson

Which example most clearly separates the intended and estimated quantity?
Where does the problem enter: measurement, sample, design, or interpretation?
Would a larger dataset solve it?
Where would your project benefit most from additional effort?


The source notes raise critiques of design-focused research. Treat them as questions about research priorities, not as a claim that all experimental designs require the same assumptions as all structural models.

title: Lecture 6.5: Evaluating Empirical Evidence
section: Statistical significance answers a limited question
text:
Statistical significance answers a limited question
A p-value is the probability, under the null model, of a test statistic at least as extreme as the observed statistic.
It is not:

The probability that the null is true.
The probability that the result will replicate.
The economic importance of the effect.

title: Lecture 6.5: Evaluating Empirical Evidence
section: Type I error, Type II error, and power
text:
Type I error, Type II error, and power



Decision
Null true
Specified alternative true




Reject null
Type I error
Correct rejection


Do not reject
Correct non-rejection
Type II error




α\alpha: probability of Type I error.
β\beta: probability of Type II error under a specified alternative.
Power: 1−β1-\beta.

title: Lecture 6.5: Evaluating Empirical Evidence
text:
Sample size changes power



Two panels from Kim showing null and alternative test-statistic distributions and different power as sample size changes.


Source: Kim; retained from Unit 6, slide 71.
With a valid fixed-level test, increasing sample size does not inherently increase the nominal Type I error rate.

Corrects the original large-sample discussion. Larger samples increase power against fixed alternatives. Misspecification, multiple testing, or interpreting tiny effects as important are separate problems.

title: Lecture 6.5: Evaluating Empirical Evidence
text:
Statistical and economic importance
A very small effect may be precisely estimated.
Ask:

What is the estimate in meaningful units?
What range is compatible with the data and assumptions?
What effect would matter for the decision?
Could the result be a precise estimate of a biased quantity?

title: Lecture 6.5: Evaluating Empirical Evidence
text:
Discussion: Kim’s diagnosis

Why does Kim object to relying on a single significance threshold?
Which concerns involve sample size, measurement, or model misspecification?
Which involve repeated testing or selective reporting?
What would a useful statistical toolbox add?

title: Lecture 6.5: Evaluating Empirical Evidence
section: Large samples do not erase bias
text:
Large samples do not erase bias
More observations can reduce variance while leaving systematic error.
MSE⁡(θ̂)=Var⁡(θ̂)+Bias⁡(θ̂)2.
\operatorname{MSE}(\hat\theta)
=\operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta)
+\operatorname{Bias}(\hat\theta)^2.

Precision can make a biased estimate look convincing.

title: Lecture 6.5: Evaluating Empirical Evidence
text:
Bayesian evidence asks another question
A Bayes factor compares the marginal likelihood of the data under two models.
Posterior odds equal prior odds times the Bayes factor.
Neither a Bayes factor nor a posterior probability is the same as a p-value. State the hypotheses and prior assumptions.

title: Lecture 6.5: Evaluating Empirical Evidence
text:
Error costs and decision thresholds
An illustrative expected-loss criterion is
L=π0CIα+(1−π0)CIIβ,
L=\pi_0 C_I\alpha+(1-\pi_0)C_{II}\beta,

where π0\pi_0 is the prior probability of the null and CI,CIIC_I,C_{II} are the costs of the two errors.
Choosing a threshold involves the decision context and the test’s operating characteristics.
Source: discussion in Kim (2019).

title: Lecture 6.5: Evaluating Empirical Evidence
section: Equivalence is not failure to reject
text:
Equivalence is not failure to reject
A nonsignificant test against zero does not establish that the effect is negligible.
Equivalence testing instead specifies a substantively meaningful interval (−Δ,Δ)(-\Delta,\Delta).
The question is whether evidence supports the effect lying inside that interval.
Choose Δ\Delta using the economic question.

title: Lecture 6.5: Evaluating Empirical Evidence
text:
Exercise: interpret two findings
Hypothetical findings:

Study A: estimated effect 0.010.01, interval [0.009,0.011][0.009,0.011].
Study B: estimated effect 1.01.0, interval [−0.2,2.2][-0.2,2.2].

What can you say about precision, compatibility with zero, and economic importance?
What units and decision context are missing?

title: Lecture 6.5: Evaluating Empirical Evidence
text:
A transparent methods section
Report:

Model and target parameter.
Sample and variable construction.
Source of identifying variation.
Controls and their justification.
Inference procedure.
Planned sensitivity analyses.

Source: Unit 6, slides 85–89.

title: Lecture 6.5: Evaluating Empirical Evidence
text:
Discussion: use both readings
A paper reports a small p-value from a large administrative dataset.
Give one question from Gibson and one from Kim that you would ask before accepting the conclusion.
Explain why each question concerns a different part of the argument.

title: Lecture 6.5: Evaluating Empirical Evidence
text:
Workshop: an evidence audit
For your proposal:

State the estimand in words.
Check whether the measure matches it.
Identify the largest source of systematic error.
Define an economically meaningful effect.
Explain how you will report uncertainty.

title: Lecture 6.5: Evaluating Empirical Evidence
text:
Before you leave
Name one conclusion that should not be drawn from a small p-value alone.

title: Lecture 7.2: Responding to Reviewers
section: Read the decision before drafting a response
text:
Read the decision before drafting a response

What did the editor decide?
Which concerns are central?
What revision is invited or required?
What deadline and submission instructions apply?

A revision invitation is an opportunity, not a guarantee of acceptance.

title: Lecture 7.2: Responding to Reviewers
text:
What rejection can teach us
Possible problems include:

Unclear contribution.
A gap between evidence and claims.
Weak organization or exposition.
Poor fit with the journal.
A substantive methodological flaw.

Separate presentation problems from problems requiring new analysis.

title: Lecture 7.2: Responding to Reviewers
text:
Discussion: Boonpramote
The reading approaches publication from editors’ and referees’ perspectives.

What makes a contribution recognizable?
How can weak communication obscure useful research?
Which concerns can be addressed through writing?
Which require changing the research itself?

Find an example in the reading for each kind of revision.

title: Lecture 7.2: Responding to Reviewers
text:
Choi: persist and listen

Read the criticism carefully.
Look for useful information even in an unwelcome report.
Treat misunderstanding as a reason to improve clarity.
Respond to substance without attacking the reviewer.

Source: Choi (n.d.).

title: Lecture 7.2: Responding to Reviewers
text:
Build a revision plan









Comment
Planned response
Manuscript change
Status




Outcome definition unclear
Define units and timing
Data section
Pending


Comparison group questionable
Investigate exposure
Analysis and limitations
Pending


Conclusion too broad
Narrow claim
Abstract and conclusion
Pending



Illustrative plan. Assign responsibility and resolve dependencies.

title: Lecture 7.2: Responding to Reviewers
text:
Answer each comment directly
For every substantive comment:

State the concern.
Explain your response.
Describe the change or provide a reasoned disagreement.
Identify where the manuscript changed.
State any remaining limitation.

Make the reviewer able to verify your answer.

title: Lecture 7.2: Responding to Reviewers
text:
When you agree

We agree that the outcome definition was ambiguous. We now specify the reference period and units in the Data section and use the same definition in Table 1.

Why is this more useful than “Fixed” or “Thank you”?
Hypothetical response example.

title: Lecture 7.2: Responding to Reviewers
text:
When you disagree

Restate the concern fairly.
Explain why the requested change would not resolve it or would change the question.
Supply evidence or reasoning.
Clarify the manuscript where misunderstanding is plausible.
Acknowledge what remains unresolved.

Disagreement should be specific and verifiable.

title: Lecture 7.2: Responding to Reviewers
text:
Discussion: Choi’s recommendations

Which recommendations improve the substance of a revision?
Which concern tone and persistence?
Which advice is context-dependent?
How would you respond if two reviewers made incompatible requests?

Distinguish general advice from a particular editor’s instructions.

title: Lecture 7.2: Responding to Reviewers
text:
Fryer: map the response
The response organizes the debate around:

What the analysis claims about racial differences and discrimination.
Selection into police-civilian interactions.
The reliability of police narratives.

Identify where the author agrees, disagrees, or clarifies the scope of a claim.
Source: Fryer (2020).

title: Lecture 7.2: Responding to Reviewers
text:
Discussion: evaluate the response
Choose one of those three issues.

What criticism is being answered?
What evidence or reasoning is offered?
Does the response change the analysis, narrow the claim, or defend the original approach?
What question would you still want answered?

Read this as an exercise in evaluating argument, not as evidence that the underlying debate is settled.

title: Lecture 7.2: Responding to Reviewers
text:
Communicate other substantive changes
Tell the editor and reviewers about important changes beyond their requests:

New data.
A different specification.
Additional checks.
Revised interpretation.

Explain why the change was made and how it affects the conclusions.

title: Lecture 7.2: Responding to Reviewers
text:
Should review correspondence be public?
The source deck raises transparency in peer review.
Discuss possible effects on:

Accountability and learning.
Candor.
Confidentiality.
Willingness to review.

What publication policy would balance these concerns?

title: Lecture 7.2: Responding to Reviewers
text:
Workshop: write a response
Use the major comment from Lecture 7.1.
Produce:

A response paragraph.
A proposed manuscript revision.
A precise location for the change.
An explanation of what remains uncertain.

Exchange with your reviewer. Can they verify that the concern was addressed?

text:

Identify your first revision task and the evidence that would show it is complete.
